title: Colloidal sphere monolayers print the DRAM honeycomb
idea: Inverts 'patterns must be printed'. Langmuir-transfer a monolayer of 40 nm silica spheres; they self-pack into the same hexagonal lattice DRAM capacitors use, are shrunk by O2/CF4 RIE and serve as the etch mask, while 180 nm stepper fences force grain boundaries onto dummy rows.
why: Sub-50 nm honeycomb with no EUV (fact 4); remaining grain defects absorbed by spare rows.

title: Femtosecond-laser self-organized ripples write maskless wordline gratings
idea: Box: Si charge x lateral access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x laser-induced periodic surface structures. A scanned femtosecond laser on a thin hardmask film self-organizes ripples with period ~lambda/4 to lambda/2 (60-200 nm) through surface-plasmon interference, giving large-area line gratings transferred as wordline or bitline arrays without mask or resist.
why: Maskless periodic patterning with a ~$300k laser most university optics labs own; risk is period uniformity, bifurcation defects and alignment, most usable for self-aligned crossbar decks.

title: Hard-disk flying heads carry plasmonic lenses for near-field array lithography
idea: Effect: surface-plasmon near-field focusing. Bowtie plasmonic apertures on surplus HDD air-bearing sliders fly 10-20 nm above a spinning 100 mm resist-coated wafer and squeeze 355 nm light into ~25 nm spots; 16 heads write periodic cell arrays in parallel. Budget: ~$400k mechanics and lasers, $300k university fab time, $300k team over 24 months.
why: Fact 4: shows sub-30 nm patterning built from mass-produced HDD parts costing dollars each, versus a $200M EUV tool; scaling to thousands of heads is the follow-on.

title: ThruChip inductive coupling replaces HBM's through-silicon via tax
idea: Keio's ThruChip Interface (inductive coils in standard metal layers) never displaced TSVs because coil area and link power looked worse at 2010 bandwidths. Put 30-50 um coils in the DRAM top metal under each channel, thin dies to ~20 um, stack with adhesive only and bring power through edge wirebonds, so no via etch, fill, reveal or keep-out zones remain.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes ~10+ TSV process steps, keep-out area and much stacking yield loss; claims ~1.5-2x more stacked bits per wafer.

title: Veneer peeling: controlled spalling yields thin dies and reusable substrates
idea: Like rotary-peeling veneer from a log, deposit a tensile Ni stressor on finished DRAM wafers and peel off a 10-20 um device layer on handle tape for stacking, then reclaim-polish and re-epi the 700 um parent substrate for up to ~5 more uses.
why: Capital and scarce resources: skips backgrind and thinning CMP and cuts quartz-crucible-dependent CZ silicon per bit several-fold.

title: One microcontact stamp sets surface energy for every ink
idea: Minify patterning to a single microcontact-printed self-assembled monolayer pattern; every following functional ink is blade-coated and de-wets into the matching wells by surface energy, self-aligned across layers.
why: Process steps and alignment: one stamp replaces several print-align steps, and cuts material waste by >90%.

title: Lehmann photo-electrochemical macropores etch capacitors without plasma
idea: Revive Volker Lehmann's 1990 photo-electrochemical macropore etching (studied by Siemens for trench DRAM): n-type silicon anodized in HF under backside LED illumination grows pores only where photogenerated holes reach the pore tips, giving straight pores of AR >150:1 from shallow seed pits. Dielectric and electrodes go in by nitrogen-purged ALD, so no step uses argon, helium or neon.
why: Fact 1 under the constraint: replaces the hardest Ar/He-diluted plasma etch with a ~$2-5M wet bench, and AR ~150 roughly doubles Cs or allows tighter pitch. Risk is pushing pore pitch below ~100 nm.

title: Aerospace anodizing grows 200:1 nanopore capacitor templates without etch
idea: Extreme user: aerospace aluminum finishing lines. Anodize a deposited aluminum film in oxalic/sulfuric acid so self-ordered nanopores (AR >200:1) grow, guided into register by a shallow imprinted pre-pattern; thin the pore-bottom barrier by voltage ramp-down, then ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN inside.
why: Capacitor wall + capital: grows the high-AR structure electrochemically in a $50k bath instead of a ~$10M HAR etcher; fluorine-free; several pores per cell multiply Cs.

title: Slow long-bitline capacity die with only two metal layers
idea: Make a second DRAM product with 1024 cells per bitline (vs ~512) and two metal layers, accepting ~50 ns access and using a low-capacitance air-gap bitline to keep sense margin; the higher cell-to-sense-amp ratio halves sense-amp count.
why: Periphery falls from ~49% toward ~30% of the die (Fact 7) and ~4 metal/via masks disappear, ~15% lower cost per bit for capacity memory.

title: Embargo engineer: BEOL-only memory tiers on existing U.S. logic lines
idea: With no front-end DRAM fab available, use only back-end tools that every mature logic fab already owns (PVD, PECVD, Cu damascene, <=400 C forming-gas anneal) to add 4-8 tiers of oxide-semiconductor 3T gain cells over finished 28-65 nm U.S. logic wafers, whose logic doubles as the periphery.
why: Converts underused U.S. mature-node BEOL capacity into memory with a ~$100-300M retrofit instead of a $15B fab, lifting U.S. manufacturability from 1-2% share. Risk: density and retention trail 1c DRAM, which is acceptable for embedded and near memory.

title: Open-licensed DRAM array IP lets any foundry make commodity memory
idea: Ideal: every fab can make DRAM. Closest: a consortium develops a proven 6F2 array plus process-module recipes validated on 2-3 foundries' tool sets and licenses them per wafer (an ARM model for memory), so logic foundries add DRAM lines without a decade of process R&D.
why: Capital/time and U.S. manufacturability: entry cost falls to tool spend only; adds suppliers to a three-vendor oligopoly.

title: Automotive microcontroller fabs: hafnium-free poly-SiON periphery wafers
idea: Carmakers' MCUs run on 40/28 nm poly-gate SiON processes in underused U.S. fabs; move row decoders, wordline drivers, I/O and control onto such a Hf-free wafer (contacts in TiN-lined Al, not W) and hybrid-bond it to the array wafer, which keeps only pitch-matched sense amps.
why: Hf-free, EUV-free periphery (facts 4, 7): much of the ~49% periphery leaves the costly array wafer, cutting array-wafer area per bit ~30-40% and putting idle U.S. mature capacity to work.

title: Container fab: kill the ballroom cleanroom
idea: Minify the cleanroom from a 100,000 m2 ballroom to sealed mini-environments around each tool inside standard shipping containers, linked by sealed-pod conveyors, so the building is an ordinary warehouse.
why: Fab construction capital: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab cost and years of build; target 3-4x faster capacity add.

title: Photochromic absorbance-modulation layer lets i-line steppers print 30 nm features
idea: Effect: reversible photochromism. A diarylethene layer over the resist is held opaque by a ring-shaped 325 nm standing wave, while 365 nm light bleaches and passes only a sub-diffraction central aperture (absorbance modulation). Recycled i-line steppers with a dual-wavelength illuminator then print dense contact arrays at 30-40 nm.
why: Fact 4: used i-line tools cost ~$1-3M versus ~$200M for EUV; could remove 1-2 EUV exposures on the periodic array contact layers.

title: Disposable nanoimprint daughter templates for periodic array layers
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying plus #27 Cheap short-living objects: write one master template by e-beam, replicate hundreds of daughter templates by imprint, and run each daughter for ~1-5k wafers on jet-and-flash imprint tools for capacitor-hole and landing-pad layers, discarding it when defects accumulate while array redundancy absorbs the rest.
why: Imprint tools cost ~1/5-1/10 of an EUV scanner and ~1/10 the power; moving 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers to NIL cuts the litho cost of those layers ~40-60% (fact 4).

title: Printing-plate family tree: replicated nanoimprint templates replace array EUV
idea: Like a record plant electroforming many stampers from one master, write a single e-beam master for the honeycomb storage-node and landing-pad layers, replicate it into ~1,000 daughter templates, and print those layers by jet-and-flash nanoimprint; each daughter is retired after a fixed wafer count before defects accumulate.
why: Fact 4 (litho capital): retires 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers; imprint tools cost ~1/5-1/10 of EUV with no source power, cutting array patterning cost per layer ~40-60%.

title: Nanosecond laser crystallization builds silicon tiers atop finished arrays
idea: Time-shift the thermal budget from furnace hours to nanoseconds: deposit amorphous Si on each finished tier and melt-recrystallize it with a ~30 ns excimer pulse seeded through small vias, so it becomes near-single-crystal while layers below stay under 400 C; repeat per tier for monolithic 3D DRAM.
why: Enables monolithic tier stacking without wafer bonding (Fact 2); each extra tier costs a deposition plus a laser pass, not a new wafer.

title: Anodized aluminum pores as self-drawn capacitor molds
idea: Po: the metal draws its own circuit. Deposit thick Al, pre-dent it with a coarse DUV hexagonal guide grid, and anodize: self-ordered alumina pores form at 25-40 nm pitch with aspect ratios >150:1 in minutes; ALD TiN/high-k/TiN into the pores makes the capacitors with no high-AR plasma etch and no capacitor-hole EUV.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) plus etch/litho capex: AR >115 reached chemically for ~1.5-2x Cs; deletes the costliest etch step and a SAQP/EUV hole layer.

title: Pre-patterned back-gate SOI wafers give temperature-tracking threshold voltage
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: the substrate supplier delivers SOI wafers with a buried back-gate grid under a thin BOX, so planar fully depleted access transistors raise their threshold by back bias as the die heats, holding 125 C leakage at 85 C levels while the fab skips its buried-wordline trench module.
why: Facts 3 and 4: moves ~10 front-end steps to a relaxed-pitch substrate process; leakage tail at 125 C cut ~10x by bias.

title: Kalundborg-style fab symbiosis with neighboring heavy industry
idea: Borrowed from the Kalundborg industrial park, where plants trade steam, water and byproducts: site a DRAM fab beside a chlor-alkali plant (byproduct H2), a steel-mill air-separation unit (N2/O2/Ar), a data center that absorbs fab waste heat and a municipal water-reclaim plant, with pipelines replacing on-site gas yards and UPW pretreatment.
why: Capital, energy and water: on-site utilities are ~15-20% of fab capex; sharing could cut that by a third and shorten fab build time by months.

title: Fe: La-Fe-Si magnetocaloric heat pumps enable dry-air heat rejection
idea: Use La(Fe,Si)13 magnetocaloric solid-state heat pumps to lift tool-coolant waste heat from ~20 C to ~50 C so it can be dumped through dry air coolers year-round, eliminating evaporative cooling towers.
why: Water: cooling-tower evaporation is often the largest consumptive water use in a fab (~25-40%) and drops to ~0. Heat-pump efficiency at scale is the risk.

title: Smoke detector: radioisotope micro-battery keeps low-leakage cells alive for decades
idea: Random stimulus 'smoke detector' (a tiny Am-241 source runs for decades) -> a Ni-63 or tritium betavoltaic cell in the module package supplies microwatts forever, refreshing an ultra-low-leakage gain-cell array whose retention is ~1000 s. Data survives loss of external power for ~decades with no new memory material.
why: Non-volatility comes from the package, with zero new process modules or fab capex. At 1000 s retention, refresh for a 16 Gb die is ~0.7 uW, which is within betavoltaic output, and the array keeps DRAM-class speed and unlimited endurance.

title: Short-loop micro-line compresses yield learning from years to months
idea: Time-shift the learning loop: a dedicated micro-line runs 30-50-step short-loop wafers containing only the module under study with 5-day cycle times, feeding fixes to the main line instead of waiting for 90-day full-flow wafers.
why: Yield ramp is where new fabs burn billions; 4-6x more learning cycles per year shortens ramp by ~12 months.

title: Atom-precise probe master cloned through a template family tree
idea: Time shift: spend weeks writing one perfect master array by parallel scanning-probe hydrogen-depassivation lithography on U.S.-built tools, then clone it through generations of imprint templates (1 -> 100 -> 10,000) so the slow atomic write is amortized over millions of wafers.
why: Sub-10 nm array templates without EUV; master cost falls below ~$0.01 per wafer.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve buys gluts and sells shortages
idea: Time-shift demand risk: a federal reserve buys U.S.-made DRAM wafers at a floor price in gluts and releases them in shortages, like the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, storing unpackaged wafers for years in nitrogen vaults.
why: Damps the boom-bust cycle that makes DRAM capital expensive; a lower risk premium could cut the cost of capital several points.

title: Continuous-flow inline fab: wafers stream under spatial process heads
idea: First principle: a DRAM wafer is actually being processed for only ~5% of its 60-90 day cycle; the rest is queueing between batch tools. Build array-module lines where single wafers ride gas bearings continuously under spatial ALD heads, spatial plasma etch heads and inline litho, like a printing press, cutting cycle time ~5x.
why: Capital and time: WIP inventory and idle tools are hidden capital; 3-5x faster learning cycles speed yield ramps.

title: Field-emitter array writes charge into an unpatterned storage film
idea: Revive the Williams tube and GE's 1970s electron-beam-addressed MOS memory (BEAMOS): a carbon-nanotube field-emitter array, each emitter with micro-deflection plates, sits ~20 um above a blank MOS storage film in sealed vacuum and writes and reads charge spots by secondary-emission contrast, regenerating them as the Williams tube did. Bit pitch is set by beam spot (~20 nm), not by lithography on the storage film.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital (Fact 4): the storage plane needs zero critical masks and no access transistor; one emitter sweeping a 50x50 um field addresses ~6M bits, moving complexity into a coarse emitter chip and cutting the 5-7 EUV array layers to none. Latency may land at 100 ns-1 us.

title: Thermos flask: NEM relay access device with vacuum-isolated storage node
idea: Random stimulus 'thermos' (a vacuum gap stops heat leaking) -> the access transistor of a DRAM-like cell is replaced by a nano-electromechanical relay whose open contact is a vacuum gap, and the storage node sits in a sealed air-gap cavity. Off-state leakage is essentially zero, so charge persists for years.
why: Turns the leakage tail into retention of years (non-volatile) and eliminates refresh and its circuitry (fact 3). Relays are made by low-temperature sacrificial release in BEOL at relaxed pitch, but contact endurance is the risk.

title: Substitute ion implanters with molecular monolayer doping and in-situ epitaxy
idea: Replace most of DRAM's ~20-30 implant steps with self-assembled dopant-bearing molecular monolayers (boron or phosphorus esters) that are capped and spike-annealed, plus selective in-situ-doped epitaxy for source/drain. Dose is set by the molecular footprint and coats 3D pillars that line-of-sight implants cannot reach.
why: Capital: removes many implanters and implant masks; conformal, damage-free junctions narrow the junction-leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Dealloyed nanoporous ruthenium sponge as the storage-node electrode
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: deposit a Ru-Al alloy into a shallow ~10:1 hole, then selectively dissolve the Al so spinodal dealloying leaves a 5-10 nm-ligament Ru sponge; conformal ALD ZrO2 and TiN then coat it, multiplying surface area 5-10x without a tall hole.
why: Trades aspect ratio for internal porosity: 5 fF in a hole ~1/4 as deep, deleting the HAR etch and support-mesh steps (facts 1, 4).

title: Electrohydrodynamic jet printing wires staircase DRAM stacks without TSVs
idea: Effect: electrohydrodynamic Taylor-cone jetting. Stack standard DDR dies in an offset staircase and e-jet print 1-2 um silver or copper nanoparticle traces down the stepped edges, forming hundreds of wide-I/O channels per die without through-silicon vias. $1M buys a commercial e-jet printer (~$200k), dies and 24 months of reliability work.
why: Fact 6: TSVs drive HBM's ~3x wafer area per bit and its yield loss; edge-wired stacks reuse ordinary DDR wafers and add high-bandwidth supply without TSV capex.

title: Build first, define later: antifuse-personalized array
idea: Reverse design-then-build: fabricate a uniform sea of cells plus an antifuse routing lattice with no product-specific decoding, test it, then program the lattice so only good subarrays are wired into the logical address map.
why: One mask set serves every density/organization SKU, removes product-specific masks and lifts effective yield; fewer mask sets and less WIP.

title: Segmented fab: array-only line plus mature-node periphery wafer
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation resolves 'leading-edge cells vs cheap periphery': run only the ~25 array-critical layers in a slim array fab, build sense amps, drivers and I/O on a 28-40 nm logic wafer bought from idle U.S. foundry capacity, and join them by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding under the mats. The array fab no longer needs high-voltage, multi-Vt or logic-metal modules.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die and ~15-20 masks; splitting cuts array-fab tool types ~30-40%, frees die area for cells (+40-60% bits/wafer) and lets U.S. foundries supply half the silicon (facts 4, 7; capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: ISO-6 ballroom fab survives on 4,096 self-repairing tiles per die
idea: Constraint: a cleanroom one to two classes dirtier than today. Wafers stay only in sealed minienvironments, and each die is 4,096 independently testable 1 Mb tiles with 20% spares and a boot-time self-test controller that remaps dead tiles, tolerating ~10x defect density.
why: Capital and time: fab shell/HVAC is ~20-25% of fab capex; halving it and cutting build time ~1 year helps U.S. manufacturability while spares hold yield.

title: Parking garage: idle 3D NAND lines build vertical 1T-nC ferroelectric stacks
idea: Random stimulus 'multi-storey parking garage' -> one access transistor at ground level with n HZO ferroelectric capacitors stacked as floors along a vertical plate pillar. It is built with the staircase, channel-hole and replacement-gate tools of 3D NAND fabs that sit idle in NAND down-cycles.
why: Non-volatile, ~1e12-1e15 endurance, ~10-50 ns. It reuses depreciated NAND capex, so near-zero new tools are needed, and 8-16 bits per transistor footprint gives a step change in density per litho layer.

title: Wet crystal-plane etch carves vertical trenches in (110) silicon
idea: Po: the crystal is the mask. On (110) wafers, align line-type array features to <112> so KOH/TMAH etching stops on vertical {111} planes, giving atomically smooth slits with AR >200:1 in a wet bench for trench capacitors or line-type 3D DRAM slits.
why: Etch capex and capacitor AR (fact 1): extreme aspect ratio at near-zero tool cost, no bowing.

title: Area-selective deposition grows landing pads where masks once went
idea: Constraint: delete three masks. Inhibitor monolayers that bind only to dielectric let ALD grow storage-node landing pads and bitline contact plugs only on exposed TiN/Si, self-aligned to the buried geometry, with a short etch-back to clear stray nodules.
why: Fact 4: eliminates the overlay-critical landing-pad EUV layer and two contact masks, ~5-8% of wafer cost and one fewer EUV pass.

title: Line-only crossbar 1S1C DRAM: OTS selector plus capacitor, SAOP-patterned
idea: Box: MIM charge x ovonic threshold switch (two-terminal) x current-pulse sensing x stackable crossbar decks x Si x self-aligned octuple patterning of lines only. Each cell is a vertical OTS in series with a small capacitor at a WL/BL crossing, so a deck is just two orthogonal line/space layers from DUV+SAOP etched into self-aligned pillars; the OTS snaps on above Vth to charge/read and its off-state holds the charge.
why: Removes hole and contact layers, the ones that force EUV (fact 4); 4F2 with two masks per deck and decks stack like cross-point so density grows without litho; risk is OTS sub-threshold leakage and threshold drift capping retention.

title: Eliminate thick-oxide I/O masks: co-packaged legacy-node DDR5 PHY chiplet
idea: Strip the I/O transistors, ESD and DLL from the DRAM die so its process needs only one gate oxide, and put the DDR5 PHY on a tiny 40 nm chiplet stacked face-to-face in the same FBGA package. Module pinout and timing stay JEDEC DDR5.
why: Removes ~3-5 masks (dual oxide, I/O implants, thick metal) and ~5-8% die area from the array process, cutting wafer cost per bit.

title: Eliminate laser fuse repair: on-die BIST and BIRA blow antifuses
idea: The die runs its own march test and built-in redundancy analysis at wafer sort and programs repair electrically into antifuses, so the laser-repair tools, their test insertion and external repair-analysis servers disappear. The host sees an ordinary DDR5 or HBM3E die.
why: Test capital: removes laser repair and a repair-test insertion (~5-10% of back-end test cost) with zero interface change.

title: Fifteen-day cycle-time capacitorless line sells memory build-to-order
idea: Ideal: memory made on demand, with no inventory or price swings. Closest: a ~30-mask capacitorless flow on single-wafer tools only (RTP instead of furnaces, no 12-hour batch ALD) targets 15-20-day fab cycle time versus ~90, and sells capacity as monthly build-to-order contracts.
why: Capital and supply: far less WIP (~$1B per fab tied up today) and supply that tracks AI demand monthly, damping 4x price spikes.

title: Laser interference gratings plus coarse cuts define the whole array
idea: Worse: insist that every array layer needs a $200M scanner and a custom reticle. Flip: expose the purely periodic wordline/bitline layers with maskless two-beam 193 nm immersion interference lithography (a ~$10-20M tool), pitch-split by SAQP, then trim with one low-resolution DUV cut mask. Arrays need periodicity, not arbitrary shapes.
why: Capital intensity: array litho tool cost drops ~10x and array masks shrink to cut layers only.

title: PCB electroless plating replaces tungsten CVD contact plugs
idea: Borrowed from PCB through-hole metallization, which plates millions of holes with no vacuum: seed DRAM bitline-contact and landing-plug holes with a Pd-activated monolayer, then electroless-plate cobalt or nickel-boron bottom-up on a wet bench, replacing WF6 CVD tungsten.
why: Scarce resource and capex: removes tungsten (China ~80%) and WF6 CVD tools; a plating bench costs ~1/10 of CVD; resistivity and voiding still need proof.

title: Module micro-fabs: one plant per process module, wafers travel
idea: Po: a fab is spread across a country. Split the DRAM flow into module plants (transistor FEOL, capacitor module, BEOL/TSV) each sized to its bottleneck tool and linked by sealed-pod wafer logistics, so capacity grows one $1-3B module plant at a time instead of a $15B integrated fab.
why: Capital lumpiness and time (fact 4): smaller capex steps, faster ramps, U.S. siting of individual modules, higher tool utilization.

title: Substitute die-to-wafer bonding with micro-transfer-printed DRAM tiles on compute
idea: Release 0.5-1 mm2 DRAM tiles from their wafer by undercutting a sacrificial layer, pick thousands at once with an elastomer stamp, and print them directly over compute tiles on the processor wafer, followed by planarization and a via step for um-scale connections.
why: Constraint: tiles ~5 um above cores give ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit access (>=10x below HBM); capital: stamps place thousands of tiles per cycle with no hybrid-bond aligner or TSVs, and tiles can come from older fabs.

title: Anodized aluminum pores template capacitors from a U.S. wet bench
idea: Swap plasma etch for slow electrochemistry: a film of U.S.-smelted aluminum is anodized for hours in acid and self-organizes into hexagonal pores with >100:1 aspect ratio, guided by a shallow imprinted dimple pattern; the alumina becomes the mold for TiN/high-k/TiN capacitor shells.
why: Replaces the hardest high-AR etch (Fact 1) with bath equipment costing ~1% of a cryo-etch tool, buildable domestically; AR 100-200:1 gives Cs ~8-10 fF.

title: Substitute plasma-etched capacitor holes with self-ordered anodic alumina pores
idea: Deposit 1-2 um of aluminum over the cell transistors, pre-dimple it with a coarse DUV pattern registered to the landing pads, then anodize in oxalic acid: pores self-order into a hexagonal lattice at a pitch set by voltage (~2.5 nm/V) with AR >100:1 in minutes. Open the pore bottoms, ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN inside, and keep the alumina as the mechanical support.
why: Facts 1 and 4: deletes the HAR etch (the slowest, costliest DRAM module) and the support-mesh patterning; AR 100-150 comes free, lifting Cs toward ~8 fF; wet anodization benches cost ~1/20 of HAR etch chambers.

title: Deli-slicer nanoskiving: film thickness, not lithography, sets line pitch
idea: Deposit a 2,000-pair laminate of alternating Mo/Ru and oxide, each exactly F thick, on a carrier block, then slice perpendicular to the layers into thin sheets whose cross-sections are atomically uniform line/space gratings ~48 um wide (one mat), and transfer the strips as wordline or bitline arrays.
why: Fact 4: replaces SAQP/EUV line patterning (3-4 litho/spacer loops) with deposition-thickness control at about +/-0.2 nm and near-zero line-edge roughness; one block yields thousands of mat strips, tungsten-free.

title: HDD bit-patterned-media block copolymers quadruple capacitor hole density
idea: Borrowed from HDD bit-patterned-media R&D, which made 1 Tdot/in2 hexagonal dot arrays by guiding PS-b-PDMS block copolymers on sparse e-beam patterns. DRAM's storage-node array is the same hexagonal honeycomb: print a 4x-sparse guide with 193i, let a high-chi BCP fill the missing holes in each unit cell, then transfer by etch.
why: Fact 4: deletes the EUV or quad-patterning step for capacitor holes and gives a near-perfect lattice with low CD variation; needs defectivity below ~0.01/cm2.

title: Substitute TSVs and microbumps with face-to-face capacitive proximity coupling
idea: Stack DRAM dies face-to-face or in a staircase so top-metal plates on neighboring dies form coupling capacitors across a ~1 um dielectric gap; data crosses as small-swing capacitive pulses with no through-silicon vias or bumps, and dies self-register with etched pits and balls.
why: Constraint: ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit versus HBM 3-4 pJ/bit (>=30x); facet: removes TSV etch/fill/reveal and microbump steps with their 20-30% yield hit and 3x area tax (fact 6).

title: Electrochromic gel images leaky storage nodes across a whole wafer
idea: Effect: electrochromic ion insertion. Before the capacitor is built, cover the exposed storage-node contacts of a test wafer with a WO3 electrochromic gel film and bias the substrate: nodes with leaky junctions pass current that darkens the film above them, so a $20k camera maps the leakage tail of millions of cells in one integrated exposure. $1M builds the test structures, gel and optics over 24 months.
why: Fact 3 and test capital: retention test takes hours on $3-5M testers; optical whole-wafer inline screening could cut that cost >5x and give fast feedback to process tuning.

title: Double-sided wafers: memory arrays on both front and back faces
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: finish a front-side array plus periphery, bond face-down to a carrier, thin to a 1-2 um etch stop, then build a second transistor/capacitor array on the backside of the same active layer, reaching the shared front periphery through nano-TSVs.
why: Doubles bits per starting wafer, halving CZ silicon and high-purity quartz crucible use per bit and sharing one periphery for two arrays (~20-25% die-cost cut; scarce resource, capital).

title: Two-faced wafers: DRAM arrays on front and back
idea: After front-side DRAM is complete, bond to a carrier, thin from the back to ~5 um and build a second array on the backside with U.S. backside-power processing know-how, sharing one periphery through nano-TSVs.
why: ~1.8x bits per crystal pulled and per substrate; the 49% periphery (Fact 7) is amortized over two arrays.

title: Edge-printed sidewall interconnects replace TSVs in HBM stacks
idea: Box: standard DRAM die x standard access x standard sensing x die stack wired on its edge x thinned Si x aerosol-jet plus laser-sintered metallization on the polished stack face. Pads routed to die edges are exposed on one face of the stack and 5-10 um pitch vertical lines are printed down that face, with capacitive face-to-face coupling carrying the fastest lanes.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV etch, fill, reveal and keep-out zones that drive ~3x area per bit and 20-30% yield loss; claims 20-40% HBM area back; risk is edge I/O density and signal integrity.

title: Eliminate the pulse-purge ALD bottleneck: rotary spatial ALD for capacitor dielectrics
idea: Deposit the ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 capacitor stack on a rotating platen that carries wafers through separated precursor and oxidant zones with long dwell for deep holes, instead of time-sequenced pulse-purge chambers. Device and DDR/HBM interface are unchanged.
why: ALD is among the most numerous DRAM tool types; spatial ALD runs ~5-10x faster per wafer, shrinking ALD tool count and floor space.

title: Carbon-mold capacitors etched with oxygen and released by dry ashing
idea: Extreme user: a closed-habitat Mars fab where HF and fluorocarbons cannot be scrubbed. Etch capacitor holes in amorphous carbon with O2/N2/COS plasma through an Al2O3 hardmask (BCl3-patterned), fill with TiCl4-based TiN and ZrO2 by ALD, then remove the mold by O2 ashing instead of an HF dip-out.
why: Capacitor wall: dry release removes the capillary forces that topple 60:1 pillars, so AR ~100:1 becomes possible (+40-60% Cs); also kills the fluorocarbon HAR etch and the HF dip.

title: HBM-thinned dies host storage capacitors on the wafer backside
idea: Extreme user: HBM stacks whose dies are already thinned to ~30 um. Build access transistors and periphery on the front, then after thinning form the capacitor array on the backside, contacted by nano-vias through ~500 nm of silicon, decoupling the capacitor thermal budget from logic-grade periphery.
why: Periphery and capacitor: periphery can use high-k/metal-gate logic (smaller, faster), the capacitor gets the whole backside area, and the thinning step HBM already pays for does double duty.

title: Reverse fab: harvest, retest and rebin retired server DRAM
idea: First principle: DRAM has effectively unlimited endurance and no dominant wear-out, so a 5-year-old die is physically almost as good as new. Build automated lines that desolder DRAM packages from retired DIMMs and boards, reball them, run full BIST, retention and row-hammer binning, and assemble certified second-life modules.
why: Supply: hyperscalers retire many exabytes of DRAM per year; recovered bits cost ~5% of new-fab capex per bit and arrive in months.

title: Combinatorial coupon line for 100x faster process learning
idea: Minify experiments to 25 mm coupons with gradient deposition and run 1000 process splits per week on a high-throughput pilot line, so new-cell development needs a $50M line, not a full fab.
why: Development time and capital: compresses 3-5 year node learning toward 1 year and lowers entry cost for US newcomers.

title: Bookbinder's peel: room-temperature spalled single-crystal silicon tiers
idea: A bookbinder peels sheets rather than sawing them. A stressed nickel film peels a ~5-10 um single-crystal silicon sheet off a donor at room temperature (controlled spalling); plasma-activated oxide bonding (<=300 C) places it, CMP thins it to ~100 nm, and a tier of Schottky NiSi source/drain transistors (<=400 C) is built; this repeats per tier, with the donor reused.
why: Gives monocrystalline access transistors on every tier without the 400-500 C split anneal of Smart Cut, and donor reuse cuts wafer use. High risk: spall roughness, thinning uniformity, low-temperature gate-dielectric quality.

title: La: LaB6 multi-cathode e-beam writes periphery without mask sets
idea: Use arrays of thousands of LaB6 cathodes in a multi-beam direct-write tool for the irregular periphery and low-volume layers, eliminating mask sets and enabling rapid design spins in a small U.S. fab.
why: Mask sets cost $10-20M per node; direct write removes them and EUV from non-repetitive layers, making a low-volume startup memory line economic.

title: Self-restoring keeper transistor makes gain cell quasi-static, refresh-free
idea: Ideal: a dynamic cell that refreshes itself. Closest: add to a 2T gain cell a minimum-size keeper transistor gated by the read node, whose subthreshold current tops the storage node up toward its own stored rail faster than the access device leaks it away, so the capacitorless cell holds data without refresh.
why: Fact 3 and Fact 4: no refresh and no leakage-tail screening, which relaxes implant/anneal control and cuts retention test time (a major test cost).

title: Relocatable fab pods: containerized modules with high resale value
idea: First principle: fab capital is expensive partly because it is stranded: a fab building cannot be moved or resold. Factory-build fab segments as sealed clean pods with minienvironment tools inside, bolt them together in months, and move, refurbish or resell them later, which lowers the risk premium on capital.
why: Capital intensity and time to capacity (3-5 years today): ~12-18 month deployment; redeployable by design.

title: Zipper: controlled spalling reuses one CZ donor for many device layers
idea: Random stimulus 'zipper' (one crack propagates cleanly) -> a stressed nickel layer is plated on the donor and a crack is propagated at a set depth to peel a few-micron device layer onto a carrier. The donor is re-polished and reused 10-20 times, and the peeled thin layers go straight into HBM stacks without grinding.
why: Scarce resources (Spruce Pine >80% of high-purity quartz crucibles): ~10x fewer Czochralski boules per bit. It also removes back-grind and thinning steps from HBM manufacturing (fact 6).

title: Factory-built cleanroom pods shrink DRAM fab build to 18 months
idea: Ideal: a fab appears overnight. Closest: standardize a 10k-wafer-per-month DRAM module as transportable prefabricated cleanroom and subfab skids, with tools installed and qualified at the module factory, then shipped and craned onto a slab; capacity grows pod by pod.
why: Capital/time: build time 3-5 years to ~1.5; smaller increments cut risk and let U.S. sites avoid megaproject labor shortages.

title: Stationary wafer, moving process heads
idea: Reverse which part moves: the wafer stays fixed on one chuck while a gantry carries in turn spatial-ALD, plasma-clean and anneal heads over it, so one station does several steps with no robot handoffs.
why: Fewer tools and transfer chambers per module, ~30% smaller footprint and higher throughput for the many deposition steps in DRAM capacitor and spacer modules.

title: Work-function-asymmetric electrodes make ZrO2 capacitors nonvolatile antiferroelectrics
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: keep the existing DRAM cylinder capacitor module but swap the top electrode for a conductor ~1 eV higher in work function (e.g., RuO2), creating a built-in field that shifts one antiferroelectric double loop to straddle zero bias, giving two remanent polarization states read through the same 1T1C sense path.
why: Nonvolatile, so zero refresh, with AFE ZrO2 endurance ~1e11-1e12; converting an existing DRAM fab needs one electrode change and no new tool types, so capex is near zero vs a new fab (facts 3, 4).

title: 1D-gridded periphery with directed-ion-beam cuts
idea: Reverse free-form layout into one-direction gratings: redesign periphery logic so every layer is a uniform line grating (ArFi plus spacer), and personalize it only with cuts made by a tilted directed ion beam through coarse openings.
why: Removes EUV and complex 2D OPC from periphery; one grating process serves all layers, so mask cost and qualification drop sharply.

title: Supercritical-CO2 release deletes capacitor support-lattice masks
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics/hydraulics: replace liquid mold-strip and drying, whose capillary forces topple tall pillars, with anhydrous mold removal and supercritical-CO2 drying; with zero surface tension, freestanding 80-100:1 pillars survive without SiN support meshes.
why: Saves the 1-2 support-lattice litho/etch steps per capacitor module and permits taller pillars (Cs toward ~7 fF) (facts 1, 4).

title: Supercritical CO2 drying lets capacitors stand without support lattices
idea: Scale insight: at the nanoscale, capillary forces from the final rinse topple tall pillars, which is why a nitride support lattice (extra deposition, litho, etch) is needed; drying in supercritical CO2 from domestic industrial gas (zero surface tension) lets freestanding pillars reach ~100:1.
why: Removes 1-2 masks and ~6 support-lattice steps; taller pillars add ~30% Cs (Fact 1).

title: Supercritical CO2 drying lets capacitors grow taller without support meshes
idea: Constraint: cut ultrapure water use 80%. Replace post-etch wet cleans and spin-dry with supercritical CO2 plus co-solvent cleaning; with zero surface tension, 100:1 capacitor pillars no longer collapse, so the support-lattice (MESH) films and their masks can be dropped.
why: Facts 1 and 4: removes 1-2 masks and lets AR rise from ~70 to ~100 (+40% Cs); fab water -80%.

title: Deposit-only cell flow by area-selective ALD with alkyl inhibitors
idea: Extreme user: an ISS-style orbital fab with almost no etch gases. Grow lines and plugs only where wanted, using non-fluorinated alkyl-silane or aminosilane inhibitor monolayers that block ALD on the dielectric, with brief Cl-based atomic-layer etch-back to clean stray nuclei.
why: Litho/capital: self-aligned additive growth removes ~2 etch+litho loops per level and fixes overlay error at critical contacts.

title: Never dice: wafer-scale DRAM module
idea: Reverse the singulate-then-assemble order: keep the whole 300 mm wafer as one memory object with on-wafer redundant mesh routing that maps around dead reticles, mounted directly as a rack-level memory sled.
why: Eliminates dicing, per-die packaging, per-die test handlers and substrate cost (~15-25% of DRAM COGS) and HBM-style TSV stacks for capacity tiers.

title: Droplet self-alignment bonds dies at 10,000 per hour
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: water droplets on hydrophilic pads pull dies into sub-0.5 um alignment by capillary force, then oxide-oxide and Cu-Cu direct bonds form in a ~250 C anneal, with no polymer and no solder to age at 125 C.
why: Facts 6 and 4: ~10x die-to-wafer throughput vs ~$5M precision pick-and-place bonders; stacked-memory back-end capex down several-fold.

title: Whole-wafer memory from an old DRAM line, never diced
idea: Po: the chip is the wafer. Run a 2x-nm DRAM flow with reticle stitching and per-reticle redundancy, keep the 300 mm wafer whole (~0.5-1 TB of bits), and bond it face-to-face to a wafer of compute or switch chiplets, skipping dicing, packaging and per-die test.
why: Packaging/test and data movement (fact 5): removes ~15-25% of cost in packaging and test; wafer-level links <1 pJ/bit; uses a depreciated fab.

title: Synaptic plasticity trimming tunes each access transistor after fabrication
idea: Synapses are wired roughly and then tuned by use; after fab, apply controlled field pulses that drift mobile hydrogen in the gate stack (or hot-carrier pulses) to raise each leaky transistor's threshold until its leakage passes a target, using the array's own sense amps as the meter.
why: Fixes the leakage tail post-fab (fact 3), cutting refresh 4-8x, and widens process windows so less inline metrology and rework is needed; est. 3-5% lower fab cost.

title: Te: thermal-threshold chalcogenide resist writes sub-diffraction imprint masters
idea: Use phase-transition mastering: a Ge-Sb-Te or incomplete-oxide resist changes phase only above a sharp temperature threshold, so a cheap 405 nm laser writer prints features ~1/4 of its spot size; selective development yields DRAM array masters for nanoimprint.
why: Master writing today needs multi-million-dollar e-beam tools and days per plate; thermal-threshold writing (Blu-ray mastering heritage) cuts master cost and time ~10x.

title: Pinecone hinges self-fold a planar array into ten stacked panels
idea: Pinecone scales fold by bilayer differential swelling; build a planar thin-film memory array on a released 1 um membrane with stress-engineered SiN/metal hinge strips between panels, then release it so the panels accordion-fold (Miura pattern) into a 10-high stack, with hinge lines carrying the bus wires to a base contact row.
why: Footprint density rises ~10x while cost per bit equals the planar process (folding is one release etch), so 10x density at the same cost per bit where package area is the limit (fact 6).

title: Strain-driven self-rolling nanomembranes form Swiss-roll capacitors per cell
idea: Box: multi-turn rolled MIM charge x planar oxide TFT x standard sensing x vertical tube x Si x stress-engineered PECVD SiNx bilayer on a sacrificial Ge layer. A flat stack (strained bilayer, metal, ALD oxide, metal) is patterned with contact litho and released, and built-in strain rolls it into a 3-5 turn tube that multiplies capacitor area 10-50x per footprint with no high-AR etch.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) solved by planar processing using PECVD, ALD and XeF2; risk is shrinking roll diameter below 200 nm (needs sub-10 nm films) and roll placement.

title: Origami memory: fold a low-resolution sheet into 3D density
idea: Worse: chase density by shrinking features with ever costlier lithography. Flip: pattern a large memory sheet on polyimide at relaxed 100+ nm rules with stress-engineered SiN/metal hinge lines, then release it and fold it accordion-style into 50-100 layers. Interconnect runs across the hinges instead of through vias.
why: Litho/capital: density by folding instead of shrinking, with DUV-only tools.

title: Diode-capacitor crossbar DRAM using NiO/Ga2O3 heterojunction diodes
idea: Revive the 1950s diode-capacitor store (a rectifier per capacitor, no transistor) as a BEOL crossbar: each crossing stacks a p-NiO/n-Ga2O3 heterojunction diode (4.8 eV gap) on a MIM capacitor, written by forward-biasing the diode and read by charge sharing with a lowered row. Layers repeat at ~2 masks each above CMOS periphery.
why: Capital and Fact 2: 4F2 per layer with no FEOL array transistor and ~2 masks per stacked layer instead of 5-7 EUV layers; ultra-wide-gap reverse leakage could stretch retention ~100x (Fact 3). Risks are diode ideality and half-select disturb.

title: Crystal casting in hollow molds: lateral selective epitaxy per tier
idea: Build the tier stack from cheap deposited oxide/nitride, carve hollow lateral oxide tubes in each tier off a vertical seed shaft, and grow single-crystal Si laterally inside them from one substrate seed by template-assisted selective epitaxy, casting all tiers' access-transistor channels in one growth run.
why: Fact 2: decouples tier count from epi stack strain, enabling 50-100 tiers on deposition tools ~1/3 the cost of superlattice epi.

title: Thinfilm's printed ferroelectric memory scaled by roll-to-roll nanoimprint
idea: Thin Film Electronics' printed P(VDF-TrFE) memory topped out at ~20-36 bits per label because it was screen-printed at ~100 um. Keep the cheap polymer and the roll-to-roll web but pattern crossbars on metallized PET by roll nanoimprint at 50 nm, then laminate 20 sheets into a block wired at its edge to a CMOS controller.
why: Meets 100x: R2R capital per m2 is ~1/1000 of a wafer fab and 50 nm 4F2 gives ~12 TB per m2 per layer; est. <$0.05/GB. Trades: us switching, 1e6-1e8 endurance, bulky form factor.

title: Antiferromagnetic Mn3Sn bits pack densely with no stray fields
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight (counterweight): each bit's antiparallel magnetic sublattices counterbalance, so cells emit no stray field and can sit edge-to-edge; spin-orbit torque from a heavy-metal line switches the noncollinear antiferromagnet in sub-ns, an antiferromagnetic tunnel junction reads it, and retention needs no power.
why: Zero refresh; the stack is ~4-6 sputtered layers vs ~15-20 for a perpendicular MTJ, with no pinned reference layers, easing deposition and etch and allowing DUV-pitch crossbars; small readout signal is the risk (facts 3, 4).

title: Reusable silicon-nitride nanostencils pattern memory layers resist-free
idea: Box: MIM charge x evaporated oxide TFT x standard sensing x 2D x any substrate x deposition through EBL+DRIE-made SiN membrane stencils. Metals, oxides and semiconductors are evaporated through aligned membrane apertures, skipping resist, develop, etch and strip, and the stencil is cleaned and reused hundreds of times.
why: Process steps and chemicals: 4-5 steps per layer collapse to one, suited to low-capex BEOL memory layers; risk is aperture clogging and edge blur below ~50 nm.

title: Monolayer doping reaches buried lateral transistors in 3D DRAM tiers
idea: Effect: self-limiting chemisorption plus solid-source diffusion. Implanters cannot reach sidewalls 20 tiers down, so flood the slit with a phosphonic- or boronic-acid monolayer that bonds to every exposed Si surface, cap it, and spike-anneal to drive 3-5 nm abrupt junctions. One wet step dopes all tiers at once.
why: Fact 2: lateral-transistor doping blocks 26+ tier 3D DRAM; replaces N tilted implant passes with one wet-bench step and removes ~$8M implanters from the line.

title: Kerfless epitaxial lift-off wafers end high-purity quartz crucible dependence
idea: Ideal: wafers without crucibles. Closest: grow 50-100 um epitaxial Si on a porous-Si release layer of a reusable parent wafer, peel and bond it to a cheap carrier, and reuse the parent 30-50 times, so one Czochralski crucible supports ~50x more wafers.
why: Resource chokepoint (Spruce Pine HPQ >80%): DRAM uses only the top few um of silicon; also cuts polysilicon energy per wafer.

title: DUV-first domestic DRAM incentive
idea: Reverse subsidy logic from 'most advanced node' to 'least chokepoint exposure': give U.S. tax credits per good bit made without EUV or China-sourced tungsten, rewarding fabs built on available DUV tools and alternative metals.
why: Redirects CHIPS-style capital toward faster, cheaper, chokepoint-free capacity; fabs can be built with tools available today.

title: DUV-guided block-copolymer honeycomb replaces EUV for capacitor array
idea: Worse: add more EUV layers to every shrink. Flip: print only a coarse DUV guide pattern, then let a cylinder-forming high-chi block copolymer self-assemble into the hexagonal lattice that the 6F2 honeycomb storage-node and landing-pad layers already use, tripling density per guide post.
why: Litho/capital (fact 4): removes 2-3 of the 5-7 EUV layers on the array (~8-12% wafer cost). Row/column redundancy absorbs DSA defectivity.

title: Self-selecting chalcogenide crossbar on a former 3D XPoint toolset
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out removes both the separate selector and the phase change: a single amorphous chalcogenide layer whose threshold voltage memorizes the polarity of the last pulse acts as selector and bit at once, built with 2 DUV masks per deck on a toolset like the one that ran 3D XPoint in Lehi, Utah.
why: Nonvolatile, so zero refresh; 4F2 per deck with stacked decks, no transistor or capacitor per bit and no EUV, reusing U.S. crosspoint know-how; ~1e9-1e10 endurance needs write buffering (facts 2, 3, 4).

title: Planar sol-gel BST capacitor, flash-lamp crystallized, ends deep etching
idea: Box: paraelectric (Ba,Sr)TiO3 charge (k~300) x standard access x standard sensing x 2D x Si x spin-on sol-gel plus millisecond xenon flash-lamp anneal. The flash crystallizes only the top ~100 nm into perovskite while the substrate stays below 400 C, so a near-planar 1:1 to 3:1 capacitor on Pt or SrRuO3 reaches ~5 fF.
why: Removes high-AR capacitor modules entirely (fact 1) with a spin coater and flash/RTP tool; risk is grain-boundary leakage and dead-layer k collapse in films under 20 nm.

title: One imprint, three layers: multi-level 3D nanoimprint
idea: Rearrange several flat exposures into one 3D stamp: an e-beam-mastered template with stepped relief imprints the storage-node landing pad, contact and line trench in one stroke, then a dual-damascene-like etch transfers it.
why: Replaces 3 critical DUV/EUV exposures with one imprint; imprint tools cost ~1/5 of EUV and use little power.

title: Laser interference lithography exposes the periodic cell lattice maskless
idea: Constraint: no litho tool may cost over $5M. A DRAM array is a perfect lattice, so expose it with 193 nm immersion four-beam interference that writes 40 nm-pitch hexagonal hole or line lattices over the full field in one flash; a conventional dry-ArF mask exposure only trims the non-periodic array edges and periphery.
why: Fact 4 capital: interference tools ~$3-5M vs $200M+ for EUV, >150 wafers/hour, no reticles for array layers; litho cost per array layer -80%.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching drills 100:1 capacitor holes wet
idea: Worse: push plasma etch to AR 115:1, with ever slower rates, bowing and twisting. Flip: pattern a perforated catalytic metal mesh and let metal-assisted chemical etching in HF/H2O2 sink the catalyst straight down at room temperature. This gives bow-free holes beyond 100:1 on a wet bench, followed by catalyst strip and clean.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) plus capital: replaces the costliest high-AR etch chamber-hours with wet benches and makes AR~115 (~1.5x Cs) reachable.

title: Split the cell across two wafers: capacitor wafer bonded on
idea: Rearrange where the cell is made: build the capacitor array alone on a cheap, relaxed-tool wafer and the access transistors on a second wafer, then hybrid-bond them face to face at sub-100 nm pad pitch so each transistor lands on its capacitor.
why: Decouples the high-AR capacitor module (no thermal or litho limits from the transistor) and lets each wafer run on its own cheaper tool set; ~20% fewer steps on the expensive wafer.

title: Sealed vacuum wafer backbone replaces the ISO-3 cleanroom ballroom
idea: Ideal: no cleanroom at all. Closest: wafers travel only through a linear vacuum/N2 tunnel that docks every tool (an extended cluster-tool backbone with mag-lev carriers), so the building needs ISO 8 air, not ISO 3-4 fan-filter ceilings, and queue-time oxidation disappears.
why: Fab capital: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab cost and a large energy/water load; est. $2-3B saved per fab and faster construction.

title: Actuarial adaptive test: warranty-priced risk replaces blanket burn-in
idea: Borrowed from insurers, who price risk statistically instead of inspecting every customer: a small team builds a model using each die's inline and probe parametrics to predict field-failure probability, skips long burn-in and retention screens for the low-risk ~80%, and backs the shipped population with a priced warranty reserve.
why: Capital: DRAM test and burn-in is ~10-15% of back-end capex and a throughput bottleneck; adaptive test can cut tester-hours 30-50%.

title: Substitute EUV with nanoimprint for periodic DRAM array layers
idea: Replace EUV exposure of the repetitive storage-node-contact, landing-pad and bitline layers with jet-and-flash nanoimprint (UV-cured resist pressed by a 1x quartz template replicated from an e-beam master); keep EUV/ArF only for irregular periphery. Imprint defects are absorbed by row/column redundancy mapped to each template's defect map, and templates rotate through a replica line.
why: Fact 4 (litho capital, single EUV supplier): an imprint tool is ~1/10 the price and power of an EUV scanner; moving 3-4 of the 5-7 EUV layers could cut litho depreciation per wafer ~30-40%.

title: Exoskeleton-molt imprint tiers: nanoimprint each monolithic memory tier cheaply
idea: Arthropods form each new cuticle against the old one; build 10 monolithic oxide-semiconductor 2T0C tiers above CMOS and pattern each tier's critical layers by jet-and-flash nanoimprint from one shared master set replicated into daughters, at ~1/8 the per-layer cost of an EUV exposure and with no scanner.
why: Ten tiers at ~1/10 the litho cost each keep total wafer cost near one EUV-patterned planar array while reaching ~10x bits/mm2 (fact 4).

title: Frozen cell: decade-long nanoimprint templates replace node chasing
idea: Constraint: one cell geometry for ten years. Pattern every array layer by jet-and-flash nanoimprint from e-beam masters replicated into hundreds of daughter templates; R&D money shifts to stacking, periphery and sensing while array litho cost collapses to template wear.
why: Fact 4: a node buys only 10-20% cost per bit; freezing it avoids ~$1-2B of litho reinvestment per node and cuts array litho cost ~80%.

title: Two-terminal DRAM cells at crossings of spacer gratings
idea: Inverts 'every cell needs a three-terminal access transistor'. Stack a vertical n+/p-/n+ punch-through selector on a planar MIM capacitor at each crossing of two orthogonal spacer-defined gratings; the selector conducts only above ~1.5 V, so half-select biasing reads and writes a 4F2 cell with no per-cell gate or contact.
why: Per-cell patterning collapses to two self-aligned line layers, 4F2 from 1990s tools; selector sub-threshold leakage sets refresh (fact 3) and is the risk.

title: Universal wafer: one mask set, late personalization for every SKU
idea: Run a single DRAM wafer design in U.S. fabs for every product and personalize at the end (I/O width, speed bin, ECC mode, density) through e-fuses, top-metal options and packaging, so the line never changes over.
why: Fewer mask sets (~$20M each), no changeover loss, higher tool utilization and faster yield learning on long single-SKU runs.

title: Purity only where electrons live: epi device layer on cheap substrate
idea: First principle: retention-critical leakage depends on defects within ~1 um of the surface, so 11N Czochralski purity in the other ~774 um is wasted. Grow a 3 um high-purity epitaxial device layer on substrates made from upgraded metallurgical-grade Si by directional solidification (no quartz CZ crucible), with a buried oxygen-precipitate getter to trap metals.
why: Scarce resources and cost: less dependence on Spruce Pine quartz crucibles and electronic-grade polysilicon; ~40-60% lower substrate cost.

title: Bamboo: grow vertical access transistors by in-situ-doped selective epitaxy
idea: Random stimulus 'bamboo' (grows in segments from a node) -> vertical channel transistors for 4F2 cells are grown, not etched: single-crystal silicon pillars are selectively epitaxied up through spacer-shrunk holes in an oxide template, switching dopant gas mid-growth to form n+/p/n+ junctions with abrupt profiles.
why: Removes the high-AR pillar etch and 2-3 implant/anneal steps. Grown sidewalls are damage-free, which narrows the leakage tail (fact 3), and the 4F2 layout gives 1.5x density over 6F2 without a node shrink.

title: SiGe quantum wells inside 3D tier stack hold the bit
idea: Ideal: the 3D DRAM's own epitaxial layers are the memory. Closest: in the Si/SiGe superlattice used to build 3D tiers, leave a thin SiGe well inside each Si channel layer as a hole pocket (~200 meV valence-band offset), turning every lateral transistor into a floating-body 1T cell so the lateral capacitor is never built.
why: Fact 2: removes the lateral-capacitor module that blocks 3D DRAM; each tier is one transistor tall, so >26 tiers come with roughly half the steps per tier.
